source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Recall of random and distorted chess positions: Implications for the theory of expertise
finding: Strong players recall game positions far better than random ones, but the skill gap shrinks a lot on random positions. Computer simulation of chunk theory matched human data.
numbers: N=25 players (5 Masters mean Elo 2395, 11 Experts 2146, 9 Class A 1890). Game vs random: F(1,22)=291.51. Skill x position type: F(2,22)=16.50. Skill effect on random positions alone not significant: F(2,22)=0.18. Chess Masters assumed to hold about 50,000 chunks.
limits: Small groups per skill level. Random-position effect was in the predicted direction but not significant here.
agent_relevance: The expert edge is mostly pattern knowledge tied to real structure, not raw capacity. An agent should expect big gains only where the input has familiar structure, and little on novel random input.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Recall of random and distorted chess positions: Implications for the theory of expertise
finding: Mirror-image reflection of real positions hurts recall by about the same amount in people and in the chunk simulation. So chunks encode which pieces sit on which squares, not abstract shape.
numbers: Mean impairment 10.3% in this experiment, against 11.4% in the simulation. Pieces correct (normal plus horizontal reflection): Masters 77.3%, Experts 49.7%, Class A 34.5%. Vertical and central modifications: 62.9%, 38.6%, 27.5%. No modification dropped recall to the random level.
limits: Contradicts Holding (1985, 1992) who argued chunks are location- and color-free. One experiment, 25 players.
agent_relevance: Retrieval cues are specific, not generic. A scaffold that stores precedents should key on concrete surface features as well as abstract schema.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Recall of random and distorted chess positions: Implications for the theory of expertise
finding: Largest recalled chunks grow with skill on game positions but not on random positions.
numbers: Largest chunk, game positions: Masters 11.2, Experts 7.4, Class A 6.2 pieces. Random positions: 4.1, 4.3, 4.1 pieces.
limits: Chunk size is inferred from placement pauses (about 2 s rule), an indirect measure.
agent_relevance: Expert advantage lives in size of retrieved units, not in a faster general-purpose memory. Retrieval units should be big and reusable.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Recall of rapidly presented random chess positions is a function of skill
finding: Re-analysis of 13 experiments found stronger players generally recall more pieces on random boards than weaker ones, though the gap is far smaller than for game positions. This overturned the textbook claim that the advantage vanishes on random material.
numbers: 13 experiments with 3-10 s presentation and 20+ pieces. Pieces correct on random boards, examples: Saariluoma 1994 Exp 1 (N=12) 3.0 vs 5.8; Saariluoma 1984 Exp 4 (N=4) 2.5, 5.0, 7.3 across three skill bands. Chase and Simon 1973 Master (2.0) did worse than the novice (3.0). Gobet and Simon 1995 saw skill gaps at all presentation times from 1 to 60 s. Reconstruction method (board, dictation, display) had no effect: F(2,27)=0.90.
limits: Most single experiments were not significant (small samples). Charness's rival idea: masters guess better. Authors reject it with data on guessing.
agent_relevance: The classic Chase-Simon random control was misread for 20 years. Do not rely on a famous null from a tiny sample (3 players).

source: Gobet & Simon (1998) Expert chess memory: Revisiting the chunking hypothesis
finding: Replication of Chase and Simon's copy and recall tasks with computer display and more players. Latency and relation patterns correlate highly with the 1973 data. The 2-second inter-chunk rule held up. Masters' chunks were larger than in 1973.
numbers: Chase and Simon (1973) tested one Master, one Expert and one Class A player. Freyhoff et al. (cited) chunk size 3.6 pieces (Masters) vs 2.7 (class B), against 2.5 vs 2.1 in 1973. 74.6% of pieces within partitions shared 3+ relations, vs 67.6% in 1973. Latency vs relations: Spearman rho -.77 (game, within glance) and -.84 (random).
limits: The 1973 Master was inactive and weak, which depressed his results. Apparatus changes (hand grasp limit) changed chunk size, so chunk size is method-dependent.
agent_relevance: The founding result replicates in structure, but sample of one per level was too thin. Treat single-case expert demos as hypotheses.

source: Gobet & Simon (1998) Expert chess memory: Revisiting the chunking hypothesis
finding: Holding and Reynolds (1982) found recall of random positions did not correlate with skill (Elo 1000-2200), but quality of move search did. Gobet argues pattern recognition runs inside search, so a memory test on the starting position misses it.
numbers: Described in the paper; no new numbers beyond the original study.
limits: Secondhand description here, original not opened. Competing account (search/SEEK-like) is not fully excluded.
agent_relevance: Rival: expertise as better search plus selective pattern use. Scaffold should let pattern retrieval feed search, not replace it.

source: Gobet & Clarkson (2004) Chunks in expert memory: Evidence for the magical number four... or is it two?
finding: A direct test that discriminates chunking theory (about 7 chunks, small chunks) from template theory (about 3 chunks, large chunks). Results favour template theory: few chunks, some very large.
numbers: Same participants on physical board and computer display, game and random boards, copy and recall. In most cases no more than 3 chunks replaced in recall. With computer display and game positions Masters replaced chunks of up to 15 pieces. Recall accuracy identical across display types. Two-second boundary supported by placement latencies.
limits: Chunk counts are derived from pause rules. Template theory adds slots, making it harder to falsify. Authors say Cowan's 4-chunk STM may be an overestimate.
agent_relevance: Working memory is small but retrieved units can be huge and slot-filled. For an agent: few active items, but each can pull in a large stored template.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Templates in chess memory: A mechanism for recalling several boards
finding: Experts recall far more pieces over several boards than 7-chunk theory predicts, so long-term retrieval structures (templates) are needed. Recall falls with each added board.
numbers: Exp 1: 3 Masters fell from 95% with 1 board to 39% with 5 boards. Cooke et al.'s 2 Masters: about 90% (1 board) to about 50% (5 boards), about 40% (9 boards). Exp 2: longer gaps between boards (2 s vs 5 s) helped. Exp 3: one Chessmaster (USCF 2396) trained over about 150 sessions, plateau near 8 boards at 60%+; percent correct rose 54.97 + 0.71 x block (r2=.51).
limits: Exp 2 had 5 subjects, Exp 3 one subject. Part of the multi-board score is explained by guessing typical piece locations (about 25% assumed).
agent_relevance: Strong evidence that expert memory is trained retrieval into long-term store, not bigger buffer. Supports external memory with fixed slots for an agent, and warns of ceiling effects.

source: Gobet (1998) Expert memory: a comparison of four theories
finding: Compares four theories (chunking, SEEK, long-term working memory, templates) on the experiments that separate them: random and distorted positions, very short presentation, interference. Chunking theory fits most data despite criticism; template theory fits best.
numbers: Qualitative comparison across many studies. Key discriminators: random-position recall, very short presentation times, interference studies.
limits: Review by a template-theory author. LTWM predicts good recall even without enough time to elaborate schemas, which is a testable point the review handles by argument.
agent_relevance: Use as map of which experiments discriminate rival accounts. Prefer designs where theories disagree.

source: Sala & Gobet (2017) Experts' memory superiority for domain-specific random material generalizes across fields of expertise: a meta-analysis
finding: Across domains the correlation between expertise level and recall of random material is moderate and positive. Chunk theories predict this (small chunks occur by chance); holistic and schema theories do not.
numbers: Overall r = .41 (abstract). After excluding two effect sizes: k=26, r=.39, 95% CI [.28,.50], I2=64.15%. Trim-and-fill (8 trimmed) gives r=.29, CI [.17,.41]. Binomial analysis: 45 studies, 55 samples, N=1,401. Meta-analysis: 24 studies, 28 samples, N=903.
limits: Publication bias evidence (asymmetric funnel). Domain (p=.116) and exposure time (p=.420) not significant moderators. Games, music, programming, sports, other.
agent_relevance: Expert edge on shuffled input survives bias correction, so a part of expertise is a big stock of small patterns. Do not assume that scrambled-input robustness comes from deep abstraction.

source: Sala & Gobet (2017) Experts' memory superiority for domain-specific random material generalizes across fields of expertise: a meta-analysis
finding: The random-material skill effect appears in many domains, not only chess, and is not moderated by exposure time or domain in this sample.
numbers: No significant moderator: Domain p=.116, Time of exposition p=.420. Sample inclusion required novices not totally unfamiliar with the material.
limits: Few effect sizes per domain outside chess. Moderator tests have low power.
agent_relevance: The small-chunk mechanism looks general, so an agent can reasonably borrow it for other domains.

source: Burgoyne, Sala, Gobet, Macnamara, Campitelli, Hambrick (2016) The relationship between cognitive ability and chess skill: a comprehensive meta-analysis
finding: Cognitive ability explains a modest share of chess skill. Fluid reasoning, comprehension-knowledge, short-term memory and processing speed all correlate about r=.22 to .25 with skill.
numbers: Gf r=.24, Gc r=.22, Gsm r=.25, Gs r=.24, average .24. Numerical ability r=.35, verbal .19, visuospatial .13.
limits: Correlations are mostly from rated samples with range restriction; chess skill measured by rating or test.
agent_relevance: Individual differences in raw ability matter, but modestly. Domain knowledge is the larger lever, which is cheap to give an agent through retrieval.

source: Burgoyne, Sala, Gobet, Macnamara, Campitelli, Hambrick (2016) The relationship between cognitive ability and chess skill: a comprehensive meta-analysis
finding: Ability matters more for children and lower-skill players than for adults and strong players. This is a boundary condition on the 'smart people become experts' account.
numbers: Gf-chess skill: youth r=.32 vs adult r=.11; unranked r=.32 vs ranked r=.14 (Q(1)=8.37, p=.004). Higher-rated (2000+) samples r=-.10 [-.34,.14] vs lower-rated r=.10 [-.04,.23], Q(1)=1.99, p=.159 (not significant).
limits: Effect for Elo cut-off was not significant. Age and ranking effects are confounded.
agent_relevance: As skill rises, general reasoning ability explains less and stored knowledge more. A weaker model with good retrieval may match a stronger model without it.

source: Gong, Ericsson & Moxley (2015) Recall of briefly presented chess positions and its relation to chess skill
finding: Chunks found with an independent repeated-recall method (not timing) differ between chess players and non-players on nearly all measures for game positions. Largest chunk size tracks rating on game positions only.
numbers: 25 rated players (mean about 1680) vs 25 non-players, 5 s display. Correlation of USCF rating with largest chunk size: r=.60 (game) vs .15 (random). Test-retest reliability of chunk count: .65 (repeated recall) vs .36 (timing technique) for game positions. Two chunk estimates correlated 0.85 or higher.
limits: No masters recruited. Players are club level, so the top end is unsampled.
agent_relevance: Chunk-size measurement can be made independent of timing. Gives a cleaner way to test whether an agent's retrieved units grow with competence.

source: Reingold, Charness, Pomplun & Stampe (2001) The perceptual aspect of skilled performance in chess: Evidence from eye movements
finding: Experts choose the best move faster and more accurately and use half the fixations. Experts look at empty squares more, which fits encoding configurations rather than single pieces.
numbers: 24 players (12 experts CFC 2100-2350, 12 intermediates). Time to best move: 11.7 s vs 23.4 s, t(22)=2.97. Correct: 4.75 vs 3.33 of 5, t(22)=2.93. Fixations per trial 44.3 vs 83.6. Saccade amplitude 4.02 vs 3.38 degrees, t(22)=2.15. Fixation duration 253 vs 244 ms, n.s.
limits: The fixation-duration result did not replicate the earlier finding by de Groot and Gobet (shorter durations for skilled players). Small N, simple tactical positions.
agent_relevance: Experts attend to fewer, more relevant things. Supports cue-first triage in the agent before any long reasoning.

source: Reingold, Charness, Pomplun & Stampe (2001) The perceptual aspect of skilled performance in chess: Evidence from eye movements
finding: Cites de Groot's finding that the best players reproduced piece locations nearly perfectly after a very brief look, and that perception and memory separated players more than search depth did.
numbers: About 93% correct for positions with about 25 pieces (de Groot). Current chunk estimate around 300,000 chunks (Gobet and Simon 2000), up from 50,000.
limits: Secondhand report of de Groot; the chunk-number estimate varies by a factor of 6 across papers.
agent_relevance: The headline 50,000 chunk number is an estimate that moved; do not hard-code it.

source: Ericsson (2019/2020) Deliberate practice and proposed limits on the effects of practice on the acquisition of expert performance
finding: Practice accounts for a variable share of skill depending on how practice is defined. A strict criterion re-analysis raises the explained variance.
numbers: Macnamara et al. (2014): practice explained 26% (games), 21% (music), 18% (sports), 4% (education), under 1% (professions); 14% overall. Ericsson's re-analysis with stricter criteria: 29% and 61% after attenuation correction.
limits: Authored by the originator of deliberate practice, so partisan. Disputed by Macnamara et al. Definition of practice drives the result.
agent_relevance: How much can be trained vs fixed is contested. Evidence that structure of practice matters supports an agent that stores lessons from graded feedback.

source: Macnamara, Hambrick & Oswald (2014) Deliberate practice and performance in music, games, sports, education, and professions: a meta-analysis
finding: Quoted via Ericsson (2019): practice explained 26% of variance in games. Meta-analysis concluded practice is important but not as important as argued.
numbers: Games 26%, music 21%, sports 18%, education 4%, professions under 1% (as quoted in the Ericsson paper that was opened).
limits: Original not opened this session. Included effect sizes disputed by Ericsson.
agent_relevance: Games (chess) show the highest practice effect, so chess results may overstate practice effects for messier real domains.

source: Chase & Simon (1973) Perception in chess / The mind's eye in chess
finding: Founding chunking study: one Master, one Expert and one Class A player; Master recalled game positions best and showed no advantage on random positions.
numbers: From later papers: Chase and Simon chunk size 2.5 pieces (Master) and 2.1 (Class A); Master recalled 2.0 random pieces vs novice 3.0 (Gobet and Simon table). n=3 players.
limits: Original not opened; numbers taken from opened secondary papers. Master was rusty. Physical board limited hand grasp.
agent_relevance: Famous result from n=3. Replicated in structure, wrong in detail about random positions and chunk size.

source: Expertise reversal effect meta-analysis (2025) A cornerstone of adaptivity: a meta-analysis of the expertise reversal effect
finding: Help that boosts novices can hurt experts. The effect is robust but asymmetric: assistance helps novices more than withholding it helps experts.
numbers: 176 effect sizes, 60 experiments, 5,924 participants. Low-knowledge learners gain from high assistance d=0.505. High-knowledge learners do better with low assistance d=-0.428. Moderators: type of prior-knowledge test, education level, domain.
limits: Abstract only read (via OpenAlex), authors not recorded. Weaker for younger students, humanities and language learning.
agent_relevance: Do not give the same scaffolding to every case. Heavy step-by-step structure may hurt on cases where the model already has strong priors (links to G1: doubt only on signal).

source: Pleiss, Schiffer & von Weizsaecker (2026) Trapped in the past? Disentangling fluid and crystallized intelligence of LLMs using chess
finding: LLM chess quality drops steadily as positions become less familiar, and falls to random-play level in out-of-distribution positions. This is the LLM version of chunk-based expertise: skill follows density of stored patterns.
numbers: 500 positions per condition (within, near, out of distribution). Average centipawn loss (ACPL): GPT-3.5 807.97, GPT-4o 540.38, GPT-5 463.5. Reported ACPL in near-distribution 4.75 higher and OOD 7.79 higher than within-distribution (as stated in text). GPT-5 illegal moves above 30% in OOD positions. All but GPT-5 on familiar positions are worse than random legal play.
limits: Single domain (perfect information). Training data not known, so familiarity is inferred from structure. Evaluated GPT lineage, claude-opus-4-6 and gemini-3-flash-preview at lowest reasoning settings.
agent_relevance: Strong parallel to expert-novice results: stored patterns drive performance. In unfamiliar cases the agent should not trust its first move; use code checks (legal moves) and tools.

source: Pleiss, Schiffer & von Weizsaecker (2026) Trapped in the past? Disentangling fluid and crystallized intelligence of LLMs using chess
finding: Reasoning (chain of thought) helps, but the gain per reasoning token shrinks as relevant priors get sparser. Scaling deepens memorised knowledge more than flexible adaptation.
numbers: Extra reasoning improved GPT-5; the relative gain per token diminished for sparse-prior positions (reported qualitatively in the text). Progress GPT-3.5 to 4o: 33.12% ACPL reduction; 4o to 5: 14.23%.
limits: Authors say reasoning mainly fixes local errors. Interpretation not proven.
agent_relevance: More thinking tokens do not replace missing patterns. Supports adding retrieval and external checks rather than only longer reasoning.

source: Ruoss et al. (2024) Amortized planning with large-scale transformers: a case study on chess
finding: A 270M-parameter transformer trained on 15 billion Stockfish-annotated data points plays at grandmaster level with no search, on boards mostly unseen in training. Memorization cannot explain it.
numbers: Lichess blitz Elo 2895 against humans; puzzle Elo up to 2867; tournament Elo 2299 vs GPT-3.5-turbo-instruct 1755 in their table. Ablations on dataset, model size, architecture and prediction target.
limits: Distilled from search-based Stockfish labels, so it learns search outputs as patterns. Gap to engine not closed by scale alone.
agent_relevance: Shows pattern recognition at scale can substitute for search when trained on verified labels. For our agent: stored verified precedents can act like expert chunks.

source: Karvonen (2024) Emergent world models and latent variable estimation in chess-playing language models
finding: A GPT trained only to predict next characters on real chess games forms an internal board state that linear probes can read and edit. It also infers player skill.
numbers: Legal move rate 99.8% (16 layers) and 99.6% (8 layers). Win rate vs Stockfish level 0 (about 1300 Elo): 46% (8 layers) and 64% (16 layers). Adding a skill vector raised win rate up to 2.6 times. The 16-layer model reaches peak probe accuracy around layer 12 vs layer 6 for 8 layers.
limits: Small model on game data, not a general LLM. Probe success does not prove the model uses the representation as humans do.
agent_relevance: Models can hold expert-like latent state without being told. Skill can be conditioned, but see persona results below.

source: Zheng et al. (2024) When 'A Helpful Assistant' is not really helpful: personas in system prompts do not improve performance
finding: Telling an LLM to act as an expert (persona in system prompt) does not reliably improve accuracy on factual questions and sometimes hurts.
numbers: 162 personas, 6 relationship types and 8 expertise domains, 4 LLM families (9 LLMs cited), 2,410 MMLU questions, 4 prompt templates. No improvement over the no-persona control overall.
limits: Only MMLU (factual multiple choice). Open-ended tasks untested. Persona type, gender and domain did change accuracy somewhat.
agent_relevance: Expertise cannot be pulled in by a label. This backs guardrail G4 (no persona voters); real expert-like gain must come from retrieved patterns and checks.

source: Gobet & Simon (2000) Five seconds or sixty? Presentation time in expert memory
finding: Cited by others: presentation time moderates expert recall; skill differences exist from 1 to 60 s, larger at long times; new chunks need about 8-10 s to form.
numbers: From opened sources: skill differences at all times from 1 to 60 s (Gobet and Simon 1995, in the 1996 paper); 8-10 s as time to create a new chunk (Sala and Gobet).
limits: Not opened. Only cited numbers.
agent_relevance: Time pressure shifts the mix of recognition vs construction. Short budgets favour recall of stored patterns.

source: Vicente & Wang (1998) Constraint attunement thesis: the expert memory advantage depends on domain structure
finding: Rival account: expert recall advantage depends on how structured the domain is, a prediction that differs from chunking.
numbers: Named as a rival theory in Gobet and Clarkson; the paper says only chunking and template theories make clear predictions about chunk size and number.
limits: Not opened. Secondhand mention only.
agent_relevance: Another reason to test claims in domains with structure vs without.

source: Ericsson & Kintsch (1995) Long-term working memory
finding: Rival account: skilled memory uses retrieval structures in long-term memory so that working memory is effectively larger. Predicts good recall even when presentation time is too short for schema elaboration.
numbers: Described in Gobet (1998, opened). No numbers read.
limits: Not opened. Gobet 1998 argues templates fit data better, but the debate is not fully settled.
agent_relevance: Direct support for letting the agent store and index intermediate state outside the context window.
